title: The supercarrier that never arrived
pull: Built for years, lost in hours

facts.text: Shinano was laid down at Yokosuka on 4 May 1940 as the third Yamato class battleship. After the loss of four carriers at Midway in June 1942, the Imperial Japanese Navy ordered her half built hull finished as an aircraft carrier.
She was the heaviest aircraft carrier yet built, a record she held until USS Forrestal was launched in 1954, and remains the largest ship ever sunk by a submarine.

Her construction was so secret that she was never officially photographed while being built. One of the very few photos of her was taken by a shipyard engineer from a tug during her sea trials in Tokyo Bay on 11 November 1944.

She was commissioned on 19 November 1944 and ordered to Kure to finish fitting out. Captain Toshio Abe asked for more time: most watertight doors were not yet fitted, compartments had not been air tested, and the crew had not trained on the pumps. The request was refused.

Shinano left Yokosuka on 28 November 1944 with the destroyers Hamakaze, Yukikaze and Isokaze, carrying 50 Ohka rocket powered suicide planes and six Shinyo suicide boats. Sources differ on the hour: one record gives departure at 1:30 p.m., others 6:00 p.m.
With no air cover available, Abe had to make the run at night instead of by day.

That evening the submarine USS Archerfish, under Cdr. Joseph F. Enright, picked her up on radar at 24,700 yards and identified her as an aircraft carrier. She was faster than the submarine, but her zigzags kept turning her back toward it.

Shinano's lookouts spotted the surfaced submarine at 10:45 p.m. Abe held his destroyers back, believing it was a decoy for a wolfpack. Soon after, an overheated shaft bearing forced the carrier down to 18 knots, the submarine's speed.
Early on 29 November Archerfish fired six Mark 14 torpedoes, set to run at 10 feet to hit high on the hull. Enright logged six hits; Japanese records count four, all on the starboard side.
Confident in his armor, Abe kept up speed, which drove more water through the holes. Flooding spread through unfinished compartments, the engines stopped, and two destroyers could not tow her.

Shinano capsized and sank at 10:57 a.m. on 29 November, less than a day after leaving Yokosuka and 10 days after commissioning. Of those aboard, 1,435 died, Captain Abe among them by his own choice; 1,080 were rescued.

At 10:00 that morning Archerfish heard a large, distant explosion. Enright wrote in his log: "Our target by all rights should have been down long ago." U.S. intelligence did not at first believe he had sunk a carrier, crediting him with a smaller 28,000 ton ship until Shinano's existence was confirmed. He received the Navy Cross.

declassified.fact: The navy hid the loss even from its own people. Shinano's survivors were quarantined on the island of Mitsuko-jima in Kure Bay until January 1945 so the news would not spread.

body:
Captain Toshio Abe asked for more time. Most of his ship's watertight doors were not even fitted. He was ordered to sail anyway.

28 November 1944. Shinano left Yokosuka for Kure with three destroyers. She was the heaviest aircraft carrier yet built, begun as the third Yamato class battleship and finished as a carrier after Midway, and so secret that she was never officially photographed while being built.

That night USS Archerfish found her on radar. Early on 29 November at least four torpedoes hit her starboard side. Flooding spread through untested compartments, and she capsized at 10:57 a.m., ten days after commissioning. Abe chose to go down with her.

U.S. intelligence at first doubted a carrier had been sunk at all.
